extracted.intended_audience: computer-science / mathematics students and authors preparing term papers and technical papers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing clear, consistent, and reader-friendly technical/academic prose (term papers, articles) in computer science and mathematics. Emphasizes grammar, organization, definitions, examples, and use of style/readability tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freewriting calisthenics (paced fluency exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep up a steady pace for five minutes without repeating yourself, without writing nonsense, and without stopping; increase the time gradually until you can do this for twenty minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as practice to develop fluency. Start short (5 minutes), avoid repetition, nonsense, and stopping; slowly increase to longer sessions (up to 20 minutes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical-trope practice (Lanham handlist exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work through Richard Lanham's Handlist of Rhetorical Terms, writing an example for every rhetorical figure listed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing one example per figure develops awareness of rhetorical devices; the author notes that merely thinking about doing it may give similar benefit and that the exercise can be somewhat shallow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Which vs. that (restrictive vs non-restrictive)
rubrics_metrics.description: "That" is the defining or restrictive pronoun, "which" the non-defining or non-restrictive; if you can substitute 'that' for 'which', do it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this rule for everyday expository prose (shirt-sleeve prose). Unnecessary use of 'which' in restrictive clauses tends to convey a bad tone and distract readers; Fowler, Strunk & White discussed and popularized these distinctions. Use judgment for literary prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone matters — many tiny choices affect readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone consists entirely of making tiny, tiny choices (e.g., which vs that); if you make enough of them wrong then you won't get your maximum readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small grammatical and stylistic errors reduce reader attention and commitment; aim to make these micro-choices carefully to maintain tone appropriate for your audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subheadings must be non-integral to running text
rubrics_metrics.description: The text should make sense if we read through it omitting the titles of subsections; subheadings should not be referred to explicitly or regarded as an 'integral' part of the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat subheadings as marginal notes or meta-level comments; avoid sentences that rely on the subheading wording for meaning (example: avoid 'Contour Integration. This technique...' when repetition makes the subheading part of the sentence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define terms clearly and early
rubrics_metrics.description: Give careful attention to definitions; define one's graph-theory (or domain) terms clearly right at the start, even the most basic ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask what background the readers share and what they may not. Define symbols and notation if they are not standard or expected by your readership (example: historically '=' had to be defined).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be consistent in terminology (especially with co-authors)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to be consistent in your use of terms; be especially careful when working with co-authors (e.g., don't use 'dominators' and 'parents' for the same concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agree on names early and avoid synonyms for a single concept; inconsistency confuses readers and suggests sloppiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't define symbols or terms you never use
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't define terms that you never use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid introducing notation or definitions that remain unused; it clutters exposition and burdens readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succinctness: "Less is more"
rubrics_metrics.description: Condense long multi-part definitions and be succinct where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorter, clearer definitions reduce intimidation and cognitive load. Trim redundant clauses and keep definitions as compact as they remain precise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simple rules to over-optimized conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a simple rule rather than an optimal one (e.g., omit an unnecessary 'j > 0' condition if it's known to hold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity aids comprehension; present the simplest correct statement that conveys the intended idea rather than a micro-optimized but confusing variant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise vocabulary to avoid ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose words that remove ambiguity (e.g., replace 'loop' by 'self-loop' when first used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch words that have multiple technical and non-technical meanings (e.g., 'left' as direction vs past tense). Reword or clarify to avoid reader confusion caused by homonyms or overloaded terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tense usage for timeless facts and algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer present tense for facts about algorithms and timeless statements (e.g., 'Gabow and Tarjan have shown...' not 'had shown...'); use past tense where appropriate for historical claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An algorithm's worst-case complexity is a timeless fact about it; reserve past tense for claims about what was known at a previous time or about historical events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation formatting should not interrupt sentence flow
rubrics_metrics.description: References should ideally be parenthetical so the sentence can be read ignoring them; avoid awkward spacing (e.g., 'Tarjan[Gab83]' is bad; prefer 'Tarjan [Gab83]' or parenthetical styles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimise disruption from citations; consider the citation style's effect on readability and whether numbering will force many later edits (Chicago caution). Use LaTeX/bibliographic tools to automate numbering issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma usage guided by speech pauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Too many commas can be a bad thing; as a rough guide, put a comma where a speaker would pause to draw breath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove unnecessary commas (example corrected placement in a sentence about graph recognition); use commas to aid rhythm and clarity rather than as mechanical insertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation and small formatting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use hyphens for adjectival compounds (e.g., 'one-vertex path' not 'one vertex path'); ensure spaces around parenthetical notes ('4.3 (below)') and use the better preposition ('vertex at distance < d' rather than 'of').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small punctuation and spacing fixes improve readability; check hyphenation for compound modifiers and maintain consistent spacing conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using unproved lemmas/theorems before they appear
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't use a lemma or theorem that is not proved until later on in the book; make it clear that proof structures respect the necessary partial ordering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you must reference a later result, explicitly indicate that the proof appears later to avoid the reader wondering whether a circular argument is being made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful use of symbols and plural/genitive forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid crowding the page with too many symbols; be cautious forming plurals and genitives of symbols (e.g., use 'each H_j is ...' or re-name constructs to avoid awkward 'Hjs descendants' which needs an apostrophe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invent clearer names if a symbol is used repeatedly; use apostrophes correctly for possessives of symbol names to avoid ambiguity and typographic ugliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ties/non-breaking spaces to avoid bad line breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ties so certain blanks are not used as line breaks (e.g., put ties after 'dominates' in 'v dominates x and x dominates w', or between 'e' and 'is' in 'if e is ...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent line breaks that distort meaning or separate word pairs that should stay together; many typesetting systems (TeX) support this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer sequences of building examples over unrelated ones
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of examples that build upon one another is much more useful than a number of unrelated examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design illustrative examples so each extends the previous, gradually increasing complexity and pedagogy rather than presenting disconnected cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use style/readability programs as prompts, not absolute judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Style programs score readability using simple formulas (average words/sentence and syllables/word) and produce grade-level estimates and other metrics; use these superficial analyses to prompt re-reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to minimise computed grade level as a rough goal, but don't overdo it—over-optimising may defeat purpose. The tools are shallow compared to human critique but can highlight issues to revisit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspect style-tool outputs (sentence lengths, passive voice, parts of speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style analysis can report average sentence length, percentage of very short/long sentences, sentence-type frequencies, percentages of nouns/adjectives/verbs, and passive-voice counts (a sentence is passive if any passive verb appears anywhere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these breakdowns to spot stylistic imbalances (e.g., too much passive voice, overuse of expletives 'It...'/ 'There...'), but interpret them in context—the tool's classifications can be crude (e.g., classifying any 'It...' sentence as an 'expletive').

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of programmatic quirks (e.g., expletive detection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some style classifiers label sentences that begin 'It ...' or 'There ...' as 'expletives', which can be a strange or misleading classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't blindly follow tool labels; understand their heuristics and verify whether flagged constructions are genuinely undesirable in your context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitative exercises for learning style (Franklin's Exercise, prosody)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises such as imitating and reconstructing passages (e.g., Franklin's method of making short hints then reexpanding them, or verse-writing and converting back to prose) can teach method, variety, and expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imitation and reconstruction to discover faults and improve expression and method. Verse exercises are hard and useful as training, but results are primarily exercises and not necessarily publishable outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider audience background when choosing level and references
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask yourself what background your readers share and what they may or may not have in common; choose terminology, explanations, and citation granularity accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If writing for an audience without high grammatical sophistication, simpler prescriptions (e.g., Strunk & White) may be appropriate; if for specialists, provide precise technical definitions and references.
